steps.t: Numbers to 10,000 Ten hundreds make a thousand , a big cube. Build the number you are asked for. thousands hundreds tens ones +1000 −1000 +100 −100 +10 −10 +1 −1 Ten hundreds make a thousand. Build a number with thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Ten hundreds make a thousand, so four places hold every number up to ten thousand. 3,406 is 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, no tens and 6 ones. Press plus 1000 three times, plus 100 four times and plus 1 six times, and the blocks show 3,406. A zero is not nothing to skip. In 3,406 it holds the tens place, and without it the number would be 346. Build the number you are asked for, starting with the biggest blocks.

What each digit is worth A digit is worth different amounts in different places . The same 8 can mean 8, or 80, or 80,000 — the column it sits in decides. Where a digit sits decides what it is worth. The same eight can mean eight, or eighty thousand. A digit is worth a different amount depending on the column it sits in. In 58 the 8 is worth 8. In 85 it is worth 80. In 80,000 it is worth eighty thousand. The digit is the same, and only its column has changed. Never read a digit on its own. Ask which column it is in before you say what it is worth. Point at the digit, name its column, then say what it is worth.

The same number, regrouped Swap one thousand for ten hundreds and you still have the same number — it is only stored differently. That swap is called regrouping , and it is what you do when you subtract. One thousand can be swapped for ten hundreds. The number has not changed, only the way it is stored. One thousand can be swapped for ten hundreds without changing the number. That swap is called regrouping. 4,208 is 4 thousands, 2 hundreds and 8 ones. Swap one thousand for ten hundreds and it becomes 3 thousands, 12 hundreds and 8 ones. It is still 4,208. Regrouping does not make the number bigger or smaller. It only changes how the number is stored. Write the number again with one fewer thousand and ten more hundreds.

Ten times, a hundred times Multiplying by 10 does not “add a zero”. Every digit moves one place to the left, and the zero only fills the gap. Multiplying by ten does not add a zero. Every digit moves one place to the left. Multiplying by ten moves every digit one place to the left. Multiplying by a hundred moves it two places. 34 times 10. The 3 tens become 3 hundreds and the 4 ones become 4 tens, so the answer is 340. 34 times 100 is 3,400. Adding a zero is not the reason it works. The digits move, and the zero only fills the empty ones place. Watch each digit move one column to the left, then read the new number.

Counting on in steps Counting on in steps of the same size works from any starting number. Find the step first — take one term away from the next — then fill the gap. Find the step from one term to the next, then use it to fill the gap. A sequence that counts on in equal steps can start from any number. 1,240, then 1,290, then 1,340. Take one term from the next: 1,290 take away 1,240 is 50. So the next term is 1,340 add 50, which is 1,390. Find the step from two terms that sit next to each other. Guessing it from the first number alone goes wrong. Take one term away from the next to find the step, then use it to fill the gap.

Below zero Temperatures can go below zero . Count down through 0 into the negative numbers. warmer +1 colder −1 The thermometer goes below zero. Count down through zero into the negative numbers. Numbers can go below zero. We call them negative numbers, and a thermometer shows them. It is 3 degrees and it gets 5 degrees colder. Count down 5 steps: 2, 1, 0, minus 1, minus 2. So it is now minus 2 degrees. Zero is a number you pass through, not a place where counting stops. Press colder one step at a time and say each number as you go.

Below zero, in order Further right on the line always means bigger — and that keeps working below zero, where −2 is bigger than −9. On the number line, further right always means bigger, even when the numbers are below zero. On a number line, further right always means bigger, even below zero. Minus 2 is to the right of minus 9, so minus 2 is the bigger number. It is only 2 below zero, while minus 9 is 9 below. Minus 9 looks bigger because 9 is a big digit, but it is further left, so it is smaller. Picture the number line, then ask which number is further to the right.

Smallest to largest Put them in order, smallest first . Watch the negatives: −9 looks bigger than −2, but it is further left , so it is smaller. Order them from smallest to largest. Below zero, the bigger the digits look, the smaller the number is. To put numbers in order, start with the one furthest left on the number line. Minus 8, minus 3, 0, 5 is in order, smallest first. Minus 8 is furthest left and 5 is furthest right. Below zero, the bigger the digit looks, the smaller the number is. Minus 8 is smaller than minus 3. Find the smallest first, then keep choosing the next one to the right.

Which one is it nearer? To round a number, find the two neighbours it sits between and ask which is nearer . Exactly halfway is the one rule you have to be told: it goes up . Rounding is asking which one it is nearer to. Find the two neighbours and compare the distances. Rounding is asking which neighbour a number is nearer to. Round 4,630 to the nearest hundred. Its neighbours are 4,600 and 4,700. It is 30 past 4,600 and 70 short of 4,700, so it rounds to 4,600. Exactly halfway is the one case that needs a rule. 4,650 is halfway, and halfway rounds up, to 4,700. Find the two neighbours, then decide which one is nearer.

One number, five answers The same number rounds to a different answer for every place you are asked about. So the question is never just “round it” — it is round it to the nearest what . One number rounds to different answers depending on which place you are asked for. One number rounds to a different answer for each place you are asked about. 47,318 to the nearest ten is 47,320. To the nearest hundred it is 47,300. To the nearest thousand it is 47,000. Always read which place the question asks for. Round it, on its own, is not a whole question. Say the place first, find the two neighbours for that place, then round.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Show what you know. Tap the answer. This is the check for big numbers and numbers below zero. You will read what digits are worth, round numbers, and put negative numbers in order. Get enough right to finish the lesson, and every answer tells you why it is right. If you fall short, press Try again. The questions come round again, and the reasons will help. For every number, name the column of each digit before you answer.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Odd, even, and what happens Pair the counters. One left over means odd . Now add two numbers and watch what the leftovers do. First number: 7 Second number: 5 Pair the counters up. If one is left over the number is odd. Now see what happens when you add two of them together. Pair up the counters. If one is left over, the number is odd. 7 and 5 are both odd, so each has one left over. Put them together and the two leftovers make a pair, so 7 add 5 is 12, which is even. Adding two odd numbers never gives an odd number. The two leftovers always pair up. Choose two numbers, add them, and watch what happens to the leftovers.

Taking away, odd and even Taking away follows a rule too, and it is the same rule: what matters is only whether each number has one left over when you pair it up. Adding is not the only thing odd and even numbers do. See what happens when you take one away from the other. Taking away follows the same rule as adding. Only the leftovers matter. 9 take away 3. Both are odd, so each has one leftover. Taking one leftover away from the other leaves none, so the answer, 6, is even. An odd number take away an odd number is even, not odd, just as when you add them. Look at whether each number has a leftover, and predict before you work it out.

steps.h: The shape that hides a number
steps.t: The shape that hides a number The shape stands for a number nobody has told you. The rest of the sum tells you what it has to be. Another one The shape stands for a number nobody has told you yet. Work out what it must be. A shape in a calculation stands for a number nobody has told you yet. 15 add triangle is 22. The triangle must fill the gap from 15 up to 22, so the triangle is 7. The shape is not a guess. The rest of the calculation decides exactly what it is. Ask what the shape has to be for the calculation to be true.

When the shape comes first The shape does not always sit in the middle. When it comes first in a take-away, it is the whole amount that is hidden — so you have to put the two known parts back together. Sometimes the shape comes first, and then it is the whole amount that nobody has told you. When the shape comes first in a take away, it stands for the whole amount. Triangle take away 14 is 30. Put the two parts back together: 30 add 14 is 44. So the triangle is 44. Do not take 14 away from 30. The triangle is the whole, so it has to be the biggest number. Put the two known parts back together to find the whole.

The same shape twice A shape stands for the same number everywhere it appears. So two of them make equal parts of the total, and a different shape is a different number. When the same shape appears twice it stands for the same number both times. A shape stands for the same number everywhere it appears. Square add square add square is 24. Three equal parts make 24, so each square is 24 divided by 3, which is 8. Different shapes can stand for different numbers, but the same shape is always the same number. Count how many times the shape appears, then share the total equally.

What comes next? Look at the step from each term to the next. Same step every time is linear . Changing step is non-linear . Find the step from one term to the next. Some sequences add the same amount every time and some do not. Find the step from each term to the next. The same step every time is linear. A changing step is non-linear. 5, 12, 19, 26. Every step is add 7, so it is linear and the next term is 33. 2, 5, 9, 14 goes up 3, then 4, then 5, so it is non-linear. Check every step, not just the first. A sequence can start like one kind and turn into the other. Work out the step between each pair of terms, then look at the steps.

Same step, or changing step? The steps are not written in this time. Work them out yourself, then say whether they stay the same — linear — or change — non-linear . Some sequences take the same step every time and some do not. Decide which this one is. This time the steps are not written in, so you work them out yourself. 4, 8, 16, 32. The steps are add 4, add 8 and add 16. They change, so it is non-linear. Going up by a lot does not make a sequence non-linear. 100, 200, 300 goes up by 100 every time, so it is linear. Take each term away from the next one, and say whether the steps stay the same.

Say the rule Finding the next term gets you one more number. Saying the rule gets you all of them. A term-to-term rule says how to get from any term to the one after it. Saying the rule out loud is worth more than one more term, because the rule gives you every term there will ever be. A term-to-term rule says how to get from any term to the next one. 2, 5, 9, 14. The steps are add 3, add 4, add 5. The rule is: add one more each time than you added before. Add 3 fits only the first step. A rule has to work for every step, not just one. Say the rule, then use it to find the next term and check that it works.

Numbers that make squares A square number is one whose dots make a perfect square. Watch what has to be added each time. Side of 4 A square number is one you can arrange into a perfect square of dots. A square number is one whose dots make a perfect square. A square with a side of 4 has 4 rows of 4 dots, which is 16. So 16 is a square number. The first four square numbers are 1, 4, 9 and 16. A square number is a number times itself, not a number times two. 4 times 4 is 16, not 8. Change the side and count the dots in the new square.

steps.h: Between one square and the next
steps.t: Between one square and the next To turn one square into the next you add an L along two edges — a side, another side, and the one dot in the corner. Count it before you count the whole square. To grow a square by one on each side you add a whole L shape round two of its edges. To grow a square by one each way, you add an L shape along two of its edges. A 6 by 6 square becomes 7 by 7 when you add 6 down one side, 6 along the other and 1 in the corner. That is 13 dots. One new row is not enough. You need a new row, a new column, and the dot in the corner. Count the L before you count the whole square.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Show what you know. Tap the answer. This is the check for odd and even numbers, missing numbers and sequences. You will find hidden numbers, decide whether sequences are linear, and use square numbers. Get enough right to finish the lesson, and every answer tells you why it is right. If you fall short, press Try again. The questions come round again, and the reasons will help. In every sequence, work out the steps before you answer.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Saying it in words Split the number into thousands , hundreds , tens and ones , and the name reads itself. Every number has a name. Break it into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones and the name reads itself. A big number reads itself once you split it into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. 7,405 is seven thousand, four hundred and five. The zero means there are no tens, so you say nothing for them. Do not say the zero out loud. We never say seven thousand four hundred and zero five. Split the number into its places, then say each part in turn.

Estimate before you work Round to something easy first. The estimate tells you roughly what to expect, so a silly answer stands out. Roughly, the answer will be about… Another one Round the numbers to something easy, work out roughly what the answer should be, and only then do it exactly. An estimate is a rough answer you work out first, so that a silly answer stands out. 387 add 214. Round them to 400 and 200. The answer should be about 600. An estimate is not the answer. You still work it out exactly afterwards. Round each number to something easy, then work with the easy numbers.

Adding it exactly The estimate told you roughly. Now do it exactly : add the ones first, and when a column makes ten or more, the ten is carried into the next column. Now do it exactly. Add the ones first, and when a column makes ten or more, carry the ten into the next column. To add exactly, start with the ones. When a column makes ten or more, carry the ten into the next column. 347 add 185. The ones make 12, so write 2 and carry a ten. The tens make 4 add 8 add 1, which is 13, so write 3 and carry a hundred. The hundreds make 5. The answer is 532. Forgetting a carried ten makes the answer too small. Write each carry above the next column so you cannot lose it. When you have an answer, check that it is close to your estimate.

Taking away exactly When a column has too little to take from, exchange one from next door — a ten becomes ten ones. What you must never do is turn the column round and take the smaller digit from the bigger. Taking away needs the opposite of carrying. When a column has too little, exchange a ten from next door. To take away, when a column has too little, exchange one from the column next door. 623 take away 187. 3 is less than 7, so exchange a ten, and 13 take away 7 is 6. The tens now hold 1, less than 8, so exchange a hundred, and 11 take away 8 is 3. Then 5 take away 1 is 4. The answer is 436. Never turn a column round and take the smaller digit from the bigger one. That gives 564, which is wrong. In each column, ask whether the top digit is big enough before you take away.

Tables, and a shortcut Every table from 1 to 10 — and a trick: in a chain of multiplications you may regroup and do the easy pair first. Multiplication can be regrouped. Choose the pair that is easy and do that one first. In a chain of multiplications you may do the easy pair first. 4 times 7 times 5. Do 4 times 5 first, which is 20. Then 20 times 7 is 140. This works for multiplying, but not for taking away or dividing. Look for a pair that makes 10, 20 or 100, and do that pair first.

Double one, halve the other Because you may regroup a multiplication, doubling one number while halving the other cannot change the answer — and it often turns an awkward sum into an easy one. Doubling one number and halving the other leaves the answer alone, and often makes the sum easy. Doubling one number and halving the other leaves the answer the same. 16 times 25. Halve 16 to get 8, and double 25 to get 50. 8 times 50 is 400, and so is 16 times 25. Doubling both numbers makes the answer four times too big. One goes up while the other goes down. Look for a number that is easy to halve, and double the other one.

Multiplying a big number Break the big number into its parts — hundreds, tens and ones — multiply each part on its own, then add them back . Every part has to be used, and forgetting the middle one is the usual slip. To multiply a big number, break it into its parts, multiply each one, and add them back together. To multiply a big number, split it into parts, multiply each part, and add them back together. 342 times 6. 300 times 6 is 1,800. 40 times 6 is 240. 2 times 6 is 12. Add them up and you get 2,052. Every part must be multiplied. Forgetting the middle part, the 40, leaves you 240 short. Write down the three parts first, then multiply each one.

steps.h: Sharing out, and what is left
steps.t: Sharing out, and what is left Take away whole groups until you cannot take another. The number of groups is the answer, and what will not make one more group is the remainder . Dividing is taking groups away until you cannot take another whole one. What is left over is the remainder. Dividing is taking away whole groups until you cannot take another. What is left is the remainder. 87 divided by 5. 17 fives make 85, and 2 are left over. So 87 divided by 5 is 17 remainder 2. A remainder must be smaller than the number you divide by. If it is bigger, you could take another group. Check it: the groups times 5, add the remainder, should give 87 again.

6s, 7s, 9s and factor pairs Every rectangle you can make from a number shows a factor pair . Pick a number to see all of them. The 6, 7 and 9 times tables, and factor pairs. Every rectangle you can make shows a factor pair. Every rectangle you can make from a number of squares shows a factor pair. 24 squares make a 4 by 6 rectangle, so 4 and 6 are a factor pair of 24. So are 3 and 8, 2 and 12, and 1 and 24. Do not stop at the first pair. Keep going until the pairs start to repeat. Pick a number and find every rectangle it makes.

Multiples and factors, both ways One fact, two names. In 6 × 4 = 24 the small numbers are factors of 24, and 24 is a multiple of each of them. Which word you use depends only on which end you are standing at. Multiple and factor are the same fact said from the two ends. The small number is a factor and the big one is a multiple. Factor and multiple are one fact said from two ends. 6 times 4 is 24. So 6 and 4 are factors of 24, and 24 is a multiple of 6 and of 4. The factor is the smaller number and the multiple is the bigger one. 24 is not a factor of 6. Say the fact as a multiplication first, then decide which end you are standing at.

Does it divide exactly? You can tell without dividing. Nearly every test only asks you to look at the end of the number. A different number You can tell whether a number divides exactly without doing the division at all. You only have to look at the end of it. You can tell whether a number divides exactly by looking at how it ends. It divides by 2 if it ends in an even digit, by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5, and by 10 if it ends in 0. It divides by 25 if it ends in 00, 25, 50 or 75, and by 100 if it ends in 00. Having a 5 somewhere in the number is not the test. Only the end of the number counts. Look at the last two digits, then try each test in turn.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Show what you know. Tap the answer. This is the check for calculating. You will estimate, add, take away, multiply and divide, and use factors and multiples. Get enough right to finish the lesson, and every answer tells you why it is right. If you fall short, press Try again. The questions come round again, and the reasons will help. Estimate first, so you know roughly what the answer should be.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

More parts, smaller parts The whole never changes. Cut it into more pieces and each piece must get smaller . Cut the bar into 4 equal parts Every size you have tried, one part of each The whole stays the same size. Cut it into more pieces and every piece has to get smaller. The whole never changes size. Cut it into more equal parts and each part must get smaller. A bar cut into 2 equal parts gives halves. Cut the same bar into 4 and each part is a quarter, half the size of a half. A bigger bottom number does not mean a bigger piece. One eighth is smaller than one quarter. Cut the bar into more parts and compare one part of each.

A fraction is a division Share the cakes fairly . What each child gets is the cakes divided by the children — and that is exactly what the fraction says. Shared between 4 children Share the cakes out fairly. The fraction each child gets is simply the cakes divided by the children. Sharing is dividing, and a fraction is a way of writing the answer. 3 cakes shared between 4 children. Each child gets 3 divided by 4, which is three quarters of a cake. The number of cakes goes on the top and the number of children on the bottom, not the other way round. Share the cakes, then say how much one child gets as a fraction.

A fraction of an amount A unit fraction is an instruction: make that many equal groups , then take one of them. of 20 A unit fraction tells you how many equal groups to make. One of those groups is the answer. A unit fraction tells you how many equal groups to make. One group is the answer. One fifth of 20. Make 5 equal groups from 20, and each group has 4. So one fifth of 20 is 4. One fifth of 20 is not 5. The 5 says how many groups to make. The answer is how many are in one group. Divide by the bottom number to find one group.

steps.h: Fractions of amounts, in real life
steps.t: Fractions of amounts, in real life A unit fraction of an amount: make that many equal groups , and the answer is what is in one of them. One quarter of 24 means share 24 into 4 equal groups. The answer is what is in one group. A unit fraction of an amount means share the amount into that many equal groups. The answer is one group. Amina has 30 mangoes and gives one fifth of them away. Share 30 into 5 equal groups, and each group holds 6. So she gives away 6 mangoes. The bottom number is how many groups, not the answer. One fifth of 30 is not 5, and it is not 25, which is what she keeps. Find the whole, divide it by the bottom number, and that is one part.

Same value, different name Two fractions can look different and be worth exactly the same . Line them up and see. Two fractions can look completely different and still be worth exactly the same. Two fractions can look different and still be worth exactly the same. One half and two quarters cover the same length of bar. So do one half and four eighths. They are equivalent fractions. Bigger numbers do not mean a bigger fraction. Four eighths is not more than one half. Line the two bars up and see whether they end in the same place.

Out of a hundred A percentage is how many parts in every hundred . The sign % is just shorthand for “out of a hundred”. Shade 25 of the 100 squares A percentage is simply how many parts in every hundred. The sign per cent means out of a hundred. A percentage is how many parts in every hundred. Per cent means out of a hundred. Shade 25 of the 100 squares and you have shaded 25 per cent. That is the same amount as one quarter of the grid. 25 per cent is not 25 things. It is 25 out of every hundred. Shade the squares you are asked for and read the percentage.

Which is bigger? Give them the same bottom number first. Then you are only comparing the top ones. Choose > , < or = . To compare two fractions, give them the same bottom number first. Then you are only comparing the top ones. To compare two fractions, give them the same bottom number first. Three quarters or five eighths? Three quarters is the same as six eighths, and six eighths is more than five eighths. So three quarters is bigger. Do not compare the bottom numbers on their own. Eighths are smaller pieces, so you need to know how many of them there are. Change one fraction so both have the same bottom number, then compare the tops.

Fractions in order Give every fraction the same bottom number . Then the top numbers tell you the order, smallest first. To put fractions in order, give them all the same bottom number, and then the top numbers put them in order for you. To put fractions in order, give them all the same bottom number first. One quarter, one half and five eighths. In eighths they are two eighths, four eighths and five eighths. Now the tops say the order: one quarter, then one half, then five eighths. Do not order them by the bottom numbers. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces, so one eighth is smaller than one half. Choose a bottom number that all the fractions can be changed into, then compare the tops.

Adding and taking away Same bottom number means the pieces are the same size , so you just count them. Estimate first , then work it out. First, estimate: will the answer be… Another one When the bottom numbers match, you are counting the same kind of piece. Guess first, then work it out. When the bottom numbers match, the pieces are the same size, so you just count them. Two fifths add one fifth is three fifths. Four sevenths take away one seventh is three sevenths. Never add the bottom numbers. The pieces are still fifths, so the bottom number stays 5. Estimate first, more or less than a whole, then count the pieces.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Show what you know. Tap the answer. This is the check for fractions and percentages. You will find fractions of amounts, spot fractions that are worth the same, and compare them. Get enough right to finish the lesson, and every answer tells you why it is right. If you fall short, press Try again. The questions come round again, and the reasons will help. For every fraction, ask what one part is worth first.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

How long is that? Every unit of time is made of a fixed number of smaller ones. Group them and you can swap between the two. How many: 3 Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour. Pick a unit and see how the smaller ones group together inside it. Every unit of time is made of a fixed number of smaller units. 60 seconds make a minute, 60 minutes make an hour and 24 hours make a day. So 3 minutes is 3 lots of 60 seconds, which is 180 seconds. Time does not go in tens or hundreds. An hour is 60 minutes, not 100. Pick a unit and see how many of the smaller unit fit inside it.

Swapping units, both ways Going to the smaller unit you multiply , because there are more of them. Going back to the bigger one you divide . It is the same fact used two ways. Swapping between units works both ways. Multiply to go to the smaller unit and divide to go back. To change to a smaller unit, multiply. To change back to a bigger unit, divide. 4 hours is 4 times 60, which is 240 minutes. 180 minutes is 180 divided by 60, which is 3 hours. Going to a bigger unit always gives a smaller number, because each unit holds more. Ask whether you are going to a smaller or a bigger unit before you choose.

steps.h: Three ways to say one time
steps.t: Three ways to say one time A clock face, a 12-hour time with am or pm, and a 24-hour time. One moment, three ways of writing it. 12-hour — 24-hour — +1 hour +5 min One moment can be written three ways. On a clock face, as a twelve hour time, or as a twenty four hour time. The am or pm tells you which half of the day it is. One moment can be shown on a clock face, as a 12 hour time, or as a 24 hour time. Twenty past three in the afternoon is 3:20 pm in 12 hour time, and 15:20 in 24 hour time. Without am or pm, a 12 hour time could be morning or afternoon. A 24 hour time never needs them. Press plus 1 hour a few times and watch all three change together.

Read the clock No numbers written out this time. The short hand gives the hour — the one it has passed , not the one it is heading for — and the long hand gives the minutes, five for every number. Now read the clock with nothing to help you. The short hand gives the hour and the long hand gives the minutes. The short hand gives the hour and the long hand gives the minutes, five for every number. The short hand is between 4 and 5, and the long hand points at the 8. The hour is 4, the one it has passed, and 8 fives are 40. So it is 4:40. Read the hour the short hand has passed, not the one it is heading for. Find the hour first, then count the minutes in fives.

Writing it in 24-hour In 24-hour time nothing is written twice, so no am or pm is needed. Morning hours stay as they are and afternoon hours have 12 added — and midnight and midday are the two you have to learn. Twenty four hour time never needs am or pm, because every hour of the day has its own number. In 24 hour time, morning hours stay the same and afternoon hours have 12 added. 9:15 am is 09:15. 3:30 pm is 15:30, because 3 add 12 is 15. Midnight is 00:00 and midday is 12:00. 12:20 am is just after midnight, so it is 00:20. It is not 12:20, and it is never 24:20. Ask am or pm first, then decide whether to add 12.

Reading a timetable Read down a column to follow one bus, and across a row to compare the same stop. Times are in 24-hour. A timetable reads down for one bus and across for one stop. Find the bus that gets you there in time. A timetable reads down a column for one bus and across a row for one stop. Follow the first bus down its column to see when it reaches each stop. Read along the library row to see when every bus gets there. Keep your finger on one row or one column. It is easy to slip onto the next line. Find your stop first, then read along its row.

Which one do you catch? Find your stop's row , then look along it for the last bus that still gets you there in time. The latest one is the answer, because any earlier one means waiting about. A timetable is only useful if you can work out which one to catch. Read across to your stop and pick the last one that gets you there in time. Catch the last bus that still gets you there in time. Buses reach the library at 09:05, 09:25 and 09:45, and you must be there by 09:30. The 09:45 is too late, so you catch the one that arrives at 09:25. The earliest bus also gets you there, but you would wait for ages. The latest one that is still in time is the one to catch. Cross out the buses that arrive too late, then pick the latest one left.

How long between? Count on from the start to the end. Do the whole units first, then the rest. Another one To find how long something lasted, count on from the start to the finish. To find how long something lasted, count on from the start to the finish. From 10:40 to 12:15. Count on 20 minutes to 11:00, then 1 hour to 12:00, then 15 minutes to 12:15. That is 1 hour and 35 minutes. Do not take the times away like ordinary numbers. An hour is 60 minutes, not 100. Count on to the next whole hour, then the whole hours, then the minutes left.

steps.h: Over the end of the month
steps.t: Over the end of the month Adding days is easy until you run off the end of the month. Use up the days that are left in this month first, and only what is over goes into the next one. Counting days past the end of a month means knowing how many days that month has. When you add days past the end of a month, you need to know how many days that month has. 28 April add 9 days. April has 30 days, so 2 days take you to 30 April and 7 days are left over. That makes 7 May. There is no 37 April. Once you pass the last day of a month, you move into the next month. Use up the days left in this month first, then carry on into the next one.

Months and years apart Gaps are not only hours and minutes. Months and years are counted the same way — and to cross from one year into another, count the whole years first and the leftover months after. Months and years are units of time too, and the gaps between them are counted the same way. Months and years are counted the same way as hours and minutes. From March 2024 to January 2026. Two whole years is 24 months, but January is two months before March, so it is 24 take away 2, which is 22 months. Count the whole years first and the leftover months after. Mixing them up gives the wrong answer. Count the whole years, then add or take away the extra months.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Show what you know. Tap the answer. This is the check for time. You will change units of time, read clocks and timetables, and work out how long things take. Get enough right to finish the lesson, and every answer tells you why it is right. If you fall short, press Try again. The questions come round again, and the reasons will help. Remember that an hour is 60 minutes whenever you count time.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

The faces of a solid Every flat face of a solid is a 2D shape you already know. Pick a solid and take it apart. Every flat face of a solid is a two dimensional shape you already know. Every flat face of a solid is a flat shape you already know. A cube has 6 faces, and every one is a square. A triangular prism has 2 triangle faces and 3 rectangle faces. A curved surface is not a flat face. A cylinder has only 2 flat faces, and both are circles. Pick a solid, take it apart, and name each face.

Fold it up: nets A net is a solid opened out flat. Fold it up in your head. What does it make? A net is a solid opened out flat. Fold it up in your head and see what it makes. A net is a solid opened out flat. Six squares joined in a cross fold up into a cube. Two circles and a rectangle roll up into a cylinder. Not every six squares make a cube. If two squares fold onto the same side, it does not work. Fold the net in your head, one face at a time.

Every line of symmetry Test each line. If folding along it makes the halves match exactly , it is a line of symmetry. Find all of them. Test each line in turn. If folding along it makes the two halves match exactly, it is a line of symmetry. A line of symmetry folds a shape into two halves that match exactly. A square has 4 lines of symmetry: one down, one across, and the two diagonals. A rectangle has only 2. A rectangle folded along its diagonal does not match, because the corners do not land on each other. Test each line in turn until you have found all of them.

Acute, right or obtuse? A square corner is a right angle , 90°. Smaller is acute . Bigger is obtuse . Turn the arm. Turn the arm. A square corner is a right angle. Smaller is acute. Bigger is obtuse. A square corner is a right angle, 90 degrees. Smaller than that is acute. Bigger is obtuse. An angle of 45 degrees is smaller than a square corner, so it is acute. An angle of 120 degrees is bigger than a right angle and smaller than a straight line, so it is obtuse. The length of the arms does not change the angle. Only the amount of turn between them matters. Turn the arm, and say acute, right or obtuse as it moves.

Putting shapes together Join shapes and you make new ones. Some shapes tessellate — they tile a floor with no gaps at all. Put shapes together and you make new ones. Some shapes tile a floor with no gaps at all. Shapes can be joined to make new shapes, and some tile a floor with no gaps at all. Two triangles join along their long side to make a square, and six triangles fitted round a point make a hexagon. Squares and hexagons tile a floor with no gaps, but circles always leave gaps. Shapes that tile must fit together at every corner, with no gaps and no overlaps. Pick two shapes, join them, and name the new shape they make.

Area without counting Count the squares once. Then find the rule that gives the same answer every time without counting. Width 5 · height 3 Count the squares once, then find the rule that gives the same answer without counting. The area of a rectangle is the number of squares inside it, and there is a rule that finds it. A rectangle 5 squares wide and 3 squares high has 3 rows of 5. That is 5 times 3, which is 15 squares. Do not add the width and the height. 5 add 3 is 8, but the rectangle holds 15 squares. Count the squares once, then check that width times height gives the same answer.

All the way round The perimeter is the distance all the way round: length + width + length + width, which is 2 × (length + width) . The perimeter is the distance all the way round. For a rectangle, add the length and the width, then double it. The perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge of a shape. A garden 7 metres long and 3 metres wide. All the way round is 7 add 3 add 7 add 3, which is 20 metres. The short way is to add the length and the width and double it. Do not multiply the length by the width. 7 times 3 is 21, and that is the area inside, not the distance round. Add the length and the width, then double the answer.

Two rectangles, one area An L shape is two rectangles joined together. Find the area of each one, then add them. An L shape is two rectangles joined together. Find the area of each one, then add them. An L shape is two rectangles joined together, so its area is their two areas added. A 5 by 3 rectangle is 15 squares, and a 2 by 2 square is 4 squares. Together the L shape covers 15 add 4, which is 19 squares. Do not treat the L as one big rectangle. The corner that is missing is not part of the shape, so its squares must not be counted. Find the area of each rectangle, then add the two areas.

steps.g: estimation fraction geometry odd and even
steps.h: An odd shape on a grid
steps.t: An odd shape on a grid An odd shape has no formula. Count the whole squares, then treat each part square as about a half. A different shape An odd shape has no rule. Count the whole squares, then pair up the part squares. An odd shape has no rule, so you estimate its area by counting squares. Count the whole squares inside the shape first. Then count each part square as about a half, so two part squares make about one whole square. Do not count a tiny sliver as a whole square. Two part squares together make about one. Count the whole squares, then pair up the part squares.

Reading between the marks When the pointer sits between two marks, the fraction of the way across tells you the reading. Move the pointer When the pointer sits between two marks, the fraction of the way tells you the reading. When a pointer sits between two marks, work out how far across it is. The marks say 200 and 300. The pointer is halfway between them, so it reads 250. Work out what each small mark is worth before you read. It is not always 1. Find the marks on either side of the pointer, then decide how far across it is.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Show what you know. Tap the answer. This is the check for shape and measures. You will name faces, fold nets, find lines of symmetry, name angles and work out areas. Get enough right to finish the lesson, and every answer tells you why it is right. If you fall short, press Try again. The questions come round again, and the reasons will help. For an area, count the rows and how many squares are in each row.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Facing and turning The four cardinal points go round in order: north, east, south, west. A quarter turn clockwise takes you to the next one. North, east, south and west. A quarter turn takes you to the next one round. The four compass points go round in order: north, east, south and west. Face north and make a quarter turn clockwise, and you face east. Another quarter turn and you face south. Clockwise goes north, east, south, west. Anticlockwise goes the other way: north, west, south, east. Say the four points in order, then make each turn one step at a time.

The eight points Between each pair sits an ordinal point, and its name is simply both names joined: north and east make north-east , written NE . Between every two cardinal points there is one more, and its name is both of theirs joined together. Between each pair of compass points sits another point, named by joining the two. Between north and east is north-east, written NE. Between south and west is south-west, written SW. North or south always comes first. We say north-east, never east-north. Name the two points on either side, then join their names.

Which way from here? Four cardinal points, and four ordinal ones in between. Follow the instruction and see where you land. North, east, south and west, and the four in between. Follow the instructions and see where you land. The eight compass points tell you which way to move. Start in the middle and move one square north-west. You land on the square that is up and to the left. A move north-east goes up and to the right at the same time. It lands on the corner square, not the one above. Follow the direction, then tap the square you land on.

Following a route A route is moves one after another . Do the first, then the second, then tap the square you land on. A route is several moves one after another. Do them in order and see where you land. A route is several moves, done one after another. From a square, go 3 east and then 2 north. You end up 3 squares to the right and 2 squares up from where you started. Do the moves in order. Only the east move changes the column, and only the north move changes the row. Do the first move, then the second, then tap the square you land on.

Coordinates Go along first, then up . Tap the point. Coordinates. Go along the bottom first, then up. Tap the point I ask for. Coordinates give the position of a point on a grid, along first and then up. The point 4, 2 is 4 along the bottom and 2 up. Start at zero, go along 4, then go up 2. Always go along first. Going up first lands you on a different point. Start at zero, go along, then up, then tap the point.

Along first, then up The first number is along , the second is up . Swap them and you are somewhere else entirely. Tap the point the label names. Coordinates always go along first and then up. Swapping them gives a different place altogether. In a pair of coordinates, the first number is along and the second is up. 2, 6 is 2 along and 6 up. 6, 2 is 6 along and 2 up. They are two different places. Swapping the numbers moves the point. 2, 6 and 6, 2 are not the same place. Say along first, then up, every time you read a pair.

The corners of a shape A shape sits on the grid and every corner has its own pair. Read the circled one: along first, then up. Every corner of a shape has its own pair of coordinates. Every corner of a shape on a grid has its own pair of coordinates. A rectangle has corners at 1, 1 and 4, 3. Its other two corners are 4, 1 and 1, 3, because each corner takes its along from one corner and its up from the other. Read each corner for itself, along from the bottom and up from the side. Do not copy another corner. Put your finger on the circled corner and read along first, then up.

Reflect it in the mirror Each square has a partner the same distance on the other side of the mirror line. Tap the squares to build the reflection. Clear Show me Every square of the shape has a partner the same distance on the other side of the mirror line. Every square of a shape has a partner the same distance away on the other side of the mirror line. A square 3 away from the line on the left has its partner 3 away on the right. A square 1 away has its partner 1 away. A reflection flips the shape over the line. It does not slide it across unchanged. Take each square in turn, count to the line, and count the same on the other side.

steps.g: geometry multiplication odd and even position
steps.h: When the mirror is the edge
steps.t: When the mirror is the edge Here the mirror line runs along the edge of the shape. Nothing has any distance to cross, so the reflection touches the original and the whole picture doubles. When the mirror sits on the edge of the shape, the reflection touches it and the whole thing doubles. When the mirror line runs along the edge of a shape, the reflection touches the shape. A square right against the mirror has no distance to cross, so its partner sits right beside it on the other side. The whole picture doubles. Do not leave a gap. There is no gap between the shape and the mirror, so there is none in the reflection. Start with the squares that touch the mirror, then do the rest.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Show what you know. Tap the answer. This is the check for direction, coordinates and reflection. You will turn to compass points, follow routes, read coordinates and reflect shapes. Get enough right to finish the lesson, and every answer tells you why it is right. If you fall short, press Try again. The questions come round again, and the reasons will help. For every pair of coordinates, go along first and then up.

Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. What would answer it? Pick a question, then decide what to collect. Some answers are groups you can name . Some are numbers you can count . What kind of data would you collect? Before you collect anything, decide what would answer your question. Some answers are groups you can name, and some are numbers you can count. Before you collect any data, decide what would answer your question. What colour do we like best is answered with groups you can name, like red or blue. How many brothers and sisters do we have is answered with numbers you count. Numbers cannot answer a question about names, and names cannot answer a question about numbers. Pick a question, then decide whether its answers are names or numbers.

Tally, then count Twenty-two children answer one at a time. Mark each one, and cross the gate on every fifth . Then count the gates. Next child Ask them all Start again Twenty two children answer one at a time. Each answer is a tally mark, and every fifth mark is a gate. A tally records answers one at a time, and every fifth mark crosses the other four like a gate. 22 children answer. Four gates make 20, and 2 more marks make 22. Mark each answer as it comes. Trying to count them all at the end is how answers get lost. Press Next child and make one mark for each answer.

One set, three pictures The same 22 answers, drawn three ways. Each one is good at something different . The same twenty two answers, drawn three ways. Each picture is good at showing something different. The same data can be drawn in different ways, and each way is good at something different. A bar chart makes it easy to compare groups at a glance. A pictogram uses a key, so one picture can stand for 2 children. A dot plot puts one dot for each answer. Read the key of a pictogram before you count. If one picture stands for 2 children, 4 pictures mean 8 children. Look at each picture in turn and say what it shows best.

Sorting two ways at once Sort 1 to 20 by two questions at once: is it even, and is it more than 10? A Venn diagram overlaps two hoops. A Carroll diagram uses four boxes. Two questions at once. A Venn diagram uses hoops that overlap. A Carroll diagram uses four boxes. Venn and Carroll diagrams sort things by two questions at once. Is it even, and is it more than 10? 12 is both, so it goes in the overlap of the two hoops. 7 is neither, so it goes outside both hoops. A number that answers yes to both questions belongs in the overlap, not in just one hoop. Ask both questions about the number, then put it in its place.

Which chart would you choose? Every chart is good at one job . Read what the child wants to show, then choose the chart that does that job. Every chart is good at one job. Choose the one that does the job the question needs. Every chart is good at one job, so choose the one that does the job you need. To count cars as they pass, use a tally chart. To see at a glance which fruit is most popular, use a bar chart. To sort by two questions at once, use a Carroll diagram or a Venn diagram. Any chart can show some data, but the wrong one hides the answer. A tally chart does not show at a glance which is biggest, and a bar chart cannot sort by two questions. Read what the child wants to show, then think which chart does exactly that.

Two classes, one question Both classes have 22 children and answered the same question. What is the same , and what is different ? Two classes, the same question, the same number of children. Look for what is the same and what is different. Comparing two sets of data means looking for what is the same and what is different. Classes 4A and 4B both have 22 children. In each class, 4 children come by car. But walking is most common in 4A, and the bus is most common in 4B. The same total does not mean the same answers. Look at every group, not just the total. Find one thing that is the same in both classes and one thing that is different.

Impossible to certain Some things cannot happen and some are sure to. Most sit somewhere in between. Put each one on the line. Some things cannot happen, some are sure to. Most sit somewhere in between. Some things cannot happen and some are sure to. Most sit somewhere in between. Rolling a 7 on an ordinary dice is impossible. The sun rising tomorrow is certain. Rolling a 6 is possible but unlikely. Something unlikely can still happen. It just does not happen very often. Put each event on the line, from impossible to certain.

Maybe, likely or certain? Impossible : it can never happen. Maybe : it might, or might not. Likely : it will probably happen. Certain : it will happen. Impossible, maybe, likely or certain. Think about what could happen, and how often. Impossible means it can never happen. Maybe means it might or might not. Likely means it will probably happen. Certain means it will happen. Musa rolling a 7 on an ordinary dice is impossible. Hodan tossing heads is maybe. Picking a red sock from 9 red and 1 blue is likely. The sun rising tomorrow is certain. Likely is not the same as certain. Even when nearly all the socks are red, the blue one could still come out. Ask yourself, could it happen, and how often would it happen, then choose the word.

steps.h: Spin it, and spin it again
steps.t: Spin it, and spin it again Four equal parts, so each should come up a quarter of the time. A few spins are lumpy. Many spins even out. Spin 10 Spin 100 Spin 1000 Spin it ten times and the counts are lumpy. Spin it a thousand times and they even out. A chance experiment gives lumpy results after a few tries, and more even results after many. The spinner has four equal parts, so each part should come up about a quarter of the time. After 10 spins one colour might come up 5 times. After 1000 spins each colour comes up close to 250 times. A few spins are not enough to tell whether a spinner is fair. Spin it 10 times, then 1000 times, and compare the counts.
